segments.text: A business pays a supplier for years. Then one email says the bank details have changed. Horos is an agent that pays invoices on Arc, and it cannot be talked into paying that new address. Not because it spots the lie, but because naming a destination is not something the contract can be asked to do.

Business email compromise cost three point zero four billion dollars last year, across twenty four thousand incidents. The usual control is to phone the supplier and confirm. That control is now under attack: deepfake voice and video impersonation of vendors was measured for the first time in twenty twenty six. Every channel a business uses to learn a new address can be synthesised, so Horos does not try to tell a real voice from a fake one.

segments.text: Here is the entire safety argument, and it fits in one function signature. pay takes a counterparty id, an amount, and a reference. There is no to parameter. The caller names who to pay, never where. The destination is read from a registry, and the only way an address becomes a counterparty's active account is a ceremony the recipient cannot complete alone.

lines.text: * @notice Pay a counterparty. The destination is not a parameter.
* @param amount          how much, in USDC base units
* @param ref             a unique reference; replaying it reverts
function pay(bytes32 counterpartyId, uint256 amount, bytes32 ref)
no `to` parameter — the caller cannot name a destination

segments.text: This is the live deployment on Arc mainnet, reading real USDC. A routine invoice releases: the address is the one already on record. Now one arrives from the same supplier, with a changed account, urgency, and an instruction not to verify. The policy holds it, and it names the sentence that gave the document away.

The site reads two chains. Mainnet runs in real USDC, signed by a local key. Testnet runs the same contracts keyless - Circle holds the only key. The page says which one you are reading, because that difference is a custody claim and not a setting.

When a supplier genuinely changes accounts, that is a ceremony. The account that was last paid agrees to be replaced. The business agrees, with a key named at registration that nobody else can use. The new account can never sign for its own arrival. The lineage is public, and it is not editable: every entry is a transaction.

None of that requires trusting the website. This reads the deployment straight from the chain, with no key and no API. Two accounts, the second replacing the first, with two signatures behind it. And the interface, checked rather than asserted: pay takes a counterparty id, and has no address parameter.
